lesson.title: England Joins the Race Across the Atlantic
lesson.summary: Spain and Portugal had a century's head start in the Atlantic, but religious rivalry with Catholic Spain, royal sponsorship, and a new way of financing risky voyages eventually pushed England into the contest for North America.
lesson.body:
For most of the sixteenth century, England was a bystander to the age of exploration. The motives that drove Spain and Portugal across the ocean, the search for gold, the desire to spread Christianity, and the hunt for a direct sea route to Asian spice markets, applied just as much to England, but the country lacked the stability to act on them. England had barely emerged from the Wars of the Roses when Henry VIII broke with the Catholic Church in the 1530s, and the decades that followed brought religious whiplash: a Protestant push under Edward VI, a violent Catholic restoration under Mary I, and finally a return to Protestantism under Elizabeth I in 1558. A kingdom absorbed in its own survival had little capacity for overseas ventures.

England's first real attempt came early and then stalled. In 1497, King Henry VII funded the Italian navigator Giovanni Caboto, known in England as John Cabot, to sail west in search of a northern route to Asia. Cabot reached the coast of North America, likely Newfoundland or Cape Breton Island, and claimed the land for England, but the crown did not follow up with settlement or sustained investment. For nearly a century afterward, English activity in the Atlantic amounted to little more than fishing voyages off Newfoundland's rich cod banks.

The picture changed under Elizabeth I. English sailors began to see the Atlantic not just as a place to claim land but as a theater for weakening Catholic Spain, England's chief rival. Sir Francis Drake raided Spanish treasure fleets and Pacific ports before completing a circumnavigation of the globe between 1577 and 1580, returning with plundered Spanish silver that made him a hero at court. Sir Humphrey Gilbert claimed Newfoundland for England in 1583, and his half brother, Sir Walter Raleigh, backed two attempts to plant a colony at Roanoke Island off the coast of present day North Carolina, in 1585 and again in 1587. The second Roanoke colony vanished entirely, its fate still debated by historians, but the effort showed that English ambitions had grown beyond raiding.

The turning point came in 1588, when England's navy and a series of storms destroyed the Spanish Armada sent to invade England. The victory did not end Spanish power, but it broke the sense that Spain controlled the Atlantic unopposed, and it freed English merchants and sailors to pursue colonization with less fear of Spanish retaliation.

What England still needed was a way to pay for colonization without bankrupting the crown. The answer was the joint stock company, a business structure that let many investors pool money and share the risk of an expensive, uncertain voyage. King James I chartered the Virginia Company of London in 1606 on exactly this model, and the company's ships reached the Chesapeake Bay the following year, founding Jamestown. English exploration, slow to start and driven as much by rivalry with Spain as by any single royal vision, had finally produced a foothold in North America.
